title: Five marks of good speech
hook: spoken at the right time, true, gentle, beneficial, with a kind heart (AN 5.198)
tomorrow: The stick in the baby's throat

segments.voice: Yesterday: samma vaca, right speech, and your line, four guards. Which guard was the sleepiest when you checked your words? Day three hundred sixty-six.

You've been rehearsing it in the shower for three days. The sentence you need to say to your roommate about the dishes, or to your father about his driving, or to a friend about the thing she keeps doing. Every version you try is either so soft it means nothing, or so sharp it'll start a fight. Long ago, the Buddha gave a checklist for exactly this moment. It has five boxes, and it would fit on a sticky note on the bathroom mirror. Today: five marks of good speech.
screen: `THE SENTENCE IN THE SHOWER.` → `TOO SOFT, OR TOO SHARP.` → `A STICKY NOTE WITH FIVE BOXES.`

segments.voice: In a short sutta in the Numbered Discourses, the Buddha says that speech with five qualities is well spoken, blameless, and not faulted by the wise. Here they are. Spoken at the right time. Spoken truly. Spoken gently. Spoken for benefit. And spoken with a mind of goodwill. Hold your shower sentence up to them and something shifts. Truth isn't first on this list. It's second. Time comes first. A true thing said at the wrong moment, in the middle of the argument, in front of the whole table, at eleven at night, can land like a stone. Gently translates the Pali saṇha: smooth, soft, fine. It's about how the words feel to receive, not only what they say. For benefit means the words are going somewhere good, for the listener, and not only for your own relief. And the last mark isn't about the words at all. It's about the heart they come from: a mind of goodwill. You could say perfectly chosen words with quiet contempt underneath, and this list would catch it. The same five turn up in the simile of the saw from a few days ago, but turned around. There the Buddha lists them as ways other people may speak to you: at the right time or not, truly or falsely, gently or harshly, helpfully or not, with goodwill or with hate. And the training is to stay steady either way. So the list cuts in both directions. It's what to aim for when you speak, and it's not a test everyone else must pass before you'll stay kind.
screen: `FIVE MARKS OF WELL-SPOKEN SPEECH.` · `TIME COMES FIRST.` · `GENTLE, HELPFUL, FROM GOODWILL.` · `THE LIST CUTS BOTH WAYS.` · then, large: `TRUE, TIMELY, KIND.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Bring back a sentence you've been rehearsing, or one you'll need to say soon. Let it play once. Now hold it to the five, slowly, a breath or two for each. Is it the right time? Is it true? Is it gentle? Will it help? Is it coming from goodwill? If one box stays empty, don't force it. Just notice which one. Then rest, and let the sentence wait in the quiet until it's ready. The bell holds the time.
Subhasita vaca, well-spoken speech. Timely, true, gentle, beneficial, and from a mind of goodwill. From the Numbered Discourses, in the book of fives.
Your line: true, timely, kind. Before one hard sentence today, ask the five questions, and notice what changes in the sentence. Day three hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often offer these five as questions to ask before speaking, and monastics hear the same five in the simile of the saw as a training in staying steady when others speak badly to them.

match.prompt: the five marks: tap the pairs.
pairs: the same five, from the other side

myth: in this list, truth comes first
the right time comes first; truth is second.
the fifth mark is about the speaker's heart, not the words
it's speech from a mind of goodwill.
the same five qualities appear in the simile of the saw
MN 21 lists them as ways others may speak to you, and trains you to stay steady either way.

fork.setup: your friend's wedding toast ran far too long. she asks how it went while the cake is being cut. what do the five marks suggest?
options: find a quiet moment later, if it would help her.
fork.reveal: AN 5.198 puts the right time first: a true word still waits for its moment, and it has to be helpful and kindly meant.

original.note: Pali subhāsitā vācā: well-spoken speech, the kind with all five marks.

trapdoor: what you thought: good speech is honest speech.
what it means: five marks: timely, true, gentle, beneficial, and from goodwill.
what a scholar hears: AN 5.198 lists kālena, saccā, saṇhā, atthasaṃhitā and mettacittena, and MN 21 reuses the same five pairs to train the listener instead of the speaker.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 21 (Kakacupama Sutta, five ways others may speak)

notes: AN 5.198 paraphrased; Pali list (kālena, saccā, saṇhā, atthasaṃhitā, mettacittena) given from memory: please confirm.
Sutta numbering of AN 5.198 differs across editions; confirm.
saṇha glossed as 'smooth, soft, fine' per standard dictionaries; 'gentle' is the usual translation in this list.
MN 21's five pairs: timely/untimely, true/untrue, gentle/harsh, beneficial/unbeneficial, with goodwill/with inner hate.
Editor review: replaced 'most of us would put truth first' (a claim about what listeners think) with the plain order of the list; otherwise checked against AN 5.198 and MN 21 and left as written.
